title: Disaggregated intelligence — koa-action, Agent Graph & AgentScript

slides.title: Disaggregated intelligence
slides.body:
Disaggregated
intelligence

Enterprise reasoning with
koa-action, Agent Graph
and AgentScript.

Reliability and cost start with
how you allocate the work.

Authored controlsAgentScript
State + transitionsAgent Graph
koa-actionBounded judgment
Reasoning modelOpen-ended work
ServicesFacts + authority
slides.purpose: Introduce disaggregated intelligence as an engineering allocation problem.
talk: System One is a useful engineering term for specialized models that answer bounded questions. It is not a claim about human cognition.
The tutorial will construct a service workflow, inspect its failure boundaries, and define how reliability, cost, and speed would be evaluated.
The Salesforce composition is proposed. Public sources do not establish a koa-action SDK, training interface, or measured benchmark.
slides.transition: First connect the architecture to the four benefits we want.

slides.title: Four benefits. One service to measure.
slides.body:
Correct outcomes

Reliability

Test decisions and enforce required checks.

Controlled variation

Predictability

Bound outputs, paths, and recovery behavior.

Less total work

Lower cost

Avoid expensive work that the case does not need.

Shorter critical path

Faster inference

Use short decision steps on frequent routes.
slides.purpose: Connect requested benefits to concrete mechanisms.
talk: Significantly lower decision cost and faster inference are the opportunity behind specialization. Their size must be established for the deployed workload.
Reliability means acceptable outcomes. Predictability includes stable output contracts and controlled paths; it is not proof that the semantic answer is correct.
The same complete customer case remains the unit of value. Extra handoffs can consume a primitive-level saving.
slides.transition: Follow one case through the rest of the tutorial.
slides.status: Mechanisms and objectives; no koa-action benchmark

slides.title: One customer, two obligations
slides.body:
“Why was I charged twice,
and why is my service down?”

One message creates two obligations.

The case ledger

InvoiceRequestedPending
OutageRequestedPending

What must survive
every transition?
slides.purpose: Establish the recurring case and its invariant.
talk: Ask the audience to name the invariant: neither request should disappear when the agent changes topics.
A task may be resolved, withdrawn by the customer, or handed off with ownership recorded. These are different statuses; handoff does not equal resolution.
This is a constructed example used to explain state and routing, not a reported customer deployment.
slides.transition: Assign an owner to each kind of work.

slides.title: Give each responsibility an owner
slides.body:
AgentScriptDefines contracts, sequencing, availability, and bound inputs
Agent GraphExecutes the workflow and retains task state
Interpretkoa-actionBounded semantic decisions
ReasonGenerative modelUnfamiliar explanations
ActBackend servicesAuthoritative facts + permissions
ReviewHuman pathWhen policy or ambiguity requires it
slides.purpose: Distinguish models, execution, configuration, and authority.
talk: AgentScript is the authoring and control language; Agent Graph is the managed runtime that executes configured behavior.
The models produce interpretations or explanations. Backend services retain authority over access and writes, while human review is an explicit branch.
The diagram denotes coordination, not ownership of every component by a model. Each case invokes only the components its configured path needs.
slides.transition: Now move process rules from prose into inspectable structure.
slides.status: Proposed composition; no native adapter asserted

slides.title: Process knowledge becomes topology
slides.body:
A process buried in instructions

Before explaining an invoice, check account access. Keep other requests pending. Retrieve the invoice first. Do not infer the balance.

Definitions and evidence still belong in node context.

Verify caller + account access
Retrieve authorized invoice facts
Explain the charge using those facts
slides.purpose: Teach which decisions, in which order, over which state.
talk: Topology encodes procedural domain knowledge: which step may run, what must precede it, and where its input facts come from.
The transformation does not remove all domain knowledge from prompts. Category definitions and authorized facts remain necessary within model calls.
A graph can enforce a poor process consistently. Review and test the topology itself.
slides.transition: Locate the runtime within the broader agent harness.

slides.title: A runtime sits beneath the harness
slides.body:
Harness

The agent loop, context strategy, tools, and operating policy.

Example in LangChain’s stack: Deep Agents.

Runtime

State transitions and the execution of the configured workflow.

Agent Graph is analogous at this layer to LangGraph.

Configuration

The authored rules and bindings that shape behavior.

AgentScript configures Salesforce’s runtime.
slides.purpose: Prevent runtime/harness/configuration conflation.
talk: LangChain distinguishes its framework, LangGraph runtime, and Deep Agents harness. The comparison helps locate responsibilities.
In this Salesforce example the configured agent is the broader harness, with Agent Graph providing runtime execution and AgentScript authoring control.
This is an architectural analogy, not LangGraph API compatibility or a claim that Agent Graph ships Deep Agents defaults. The public AgentScript repo contains tooling, not the managed runtime.
slides.transition: Define the first decision before selecting its integration.

slides.title: Start with a decision contract
slides.body:
Question

Which service route
is supported now?

Read the conversation so far
and the relevant service context.

Version the question and category definitions.

Allowed answers

billingtechnicalaccount_accessmixedunclear
Unusable or ambiguous result

Clarify within a budget,
then use an explicit handoff.
slides.purpose: Give a bounded task a testable contract.
talk: The labels are application choices, not a documented koa-action response schema. Mixed and unclear are first-class outcomes.
Provide positive and negative examples at the category boundaries. The same contract controls labeling and evaluation.
A timeout or malformed result must not default into a business transaction. Specify its fallback separately from semantic ambiguity.
slides.transition: Match the question to the right primitive.

slides.title: Four bounded decisions, four contracts
slides.body:
01

Classification

Which route?

Select a category.

02

Noul

Cancellation requested?

Assess a yes/no proposition.

03

Scoring

How urgent?

Use an anchored rubric.

04

Endpointing

Has the turn ended?

Judge the available prefix.
slides.purpose: Cover the four user-specified koa-action capabilities.
talk: The user brief supplies classification, noul, scoring, and semantic endpointing as koa-action capabilities.
TypeSafe documents analogous decision concepts, but its SDK fields, batching, calibration, and training claims do not define a Salesforce interface.
Each primitive needs its own target and error measure. A rubric score and the probability of a binary proposition are not interchangeable.
slides.transition: Make that semantic distinction tangible.
slides.status: koa-action capabilities: supplied brief; interfaces unspecified

slides.title: Probability and intensity answer different questions
slides.body:
Noul · TypeSafe semantics

Was cancellation requested?

A probability-valued
yes/no judgment.

An uncertain answer does not mean
“a medium amount of cancellation.”

Score · illustrative rubric

How urgent is the issue?

Can wait

Work disrupted

Critical service blocked
slides.purpose: Explain binary proposition estimates versus severity rubrics.
talk: TypeSafe’s Noul is the probability of the yes answer; its Score uses ordered rubric levels and can be fractional.
A mean rubric score can hide different distributions. Preserve the output meaning that the downstream rule actually uses.
The corresponding koa-action fields, ranges, and calibration require their own verified contract. No numeric Salesforce response is shown here.
slides.transition: A decision about when to respond has an additional time boundary.

slides.title: Endpointing is a decision in time
slides.body:
Available audio prefixFuture audioDecision now

Cut too early

The customer is interrupted.

Wait too long

The response is delayed.

Keep the boundary

Future audio supplies labels only.
slides.purpose: Explain semantic endpointing and temporal leakage.
talk: The waveform is illustrative. The task asks whether a spoken turn has ended using only the available prefix.
Future speech may establish the reference label, but it must not become part of the earlier input.
Measure premature cutoff and delay separately. Keep all prefixes of a conversation together when splitting data.
slides.transition: Next decide which decisions may run in parallel.

slides.title: Split work along information dependencies
slides.body:
Same decision-time snapshot
IntentWhich route?
CancellationRequested or not?
Independent execution can still produce correlated errors.
Verify account access
Retrieve invoice facts
Explain the invoice
slides.purpose: Separate execution independence from causality.
talk: Independent questions can read the same snapshot; a later step that needs a new fact must wait for that fact.
This is a workflow-design pattern, not a claim about a native koa-action batching API.
Parallel question execution does not imply statistically independent errors. Missing evidence can affect several judgments at once.
slides.transition: Make each node’s evidence window explicit.

slides.title: Each node sees a different view of the case
slides.body:
Case stateConversation

Trusted identity

Invoice facts

Pending tasks
Route decisionReads the request + category definitions
Access checkReads trusted principal + account relationship
ExplanationReads the request + authorized invoice facts
slides.purpose: Teach context boundaries as authored data dependencies.
talk: Graph design determines what information exists before a node runs and which part of state it receives.
A customer-provided account identifier does not become a verified identity because it appears in a model output.
Narrowing context can reduce unnecessary processing, but removing a required fact can reduce quality. Version and evaluate the context selection.
slides.transition: Use that state to preserve the mixed request.

slides.title: State preserves work across a branch
slides.body:
Route = mixedBoth requests retained
Clarify priorityCustomer chooses billing
Billing activeExplain, then check resolution
Outage pendingResume or record explicit reprioritization
Clarification budgetThen a recorded handoff
slides.purpose: Make persistent obligations visible.
talk: The application records requested, active, resolved, and handed-off task states separately.
An explanation is an event, not a proof of resolution. The completion rule should reference the actual business outcome or customer confirmation.
The clarification loop has a time or turn budget. A handoff retains outstanding work and receiving ownership.
slides.transition: This is where neural interpretation meets explicit control.

slides.title: Guided determinism gives uncertainty a place
slides.body:
Neural interpretation
inside an authored process.
AgentScript defines where model choice is available.
Agent Graph executes the configured transitions.

Interpretation

Fallible semantic judgment.

Procedure

Required steps and state changes.

Authority

Enforced by trusted services.
slides.purpose: Explain neuro-symbolic reasoning in plain terms.
talk: Neuro-symbolic reasoning combines learned interpretation with explicit software rules and state.
Guided determinism describes constraints on the effect of model judgments. It does not guarantee perfect classification, identical prose, or eventual completion.
The configuration and the model can evolve independently when their boundary is explicit and tested.
slides.transition: Three AgentScript concepts make that boundary concrete.

slides.title: Availability and required execution differ
slides.body:
The service boundary

A model signal
cannot grant
account access.

The backend rechecks
the caller and policy
before a write.

Required work

run / procedure

Use explicit procedure logic for checks that must execute.

Permitted choices

available when

Filter which actions the model may select. Availability does not force selection.

Controlled arguments

with / bound input

Bind consequential inputs from trusted state.
slides.purpose: Teach precise AgentScript control semantics.
talk: These are language constructs, not a runnable integration. Action definitions, dialect, and deployment configuration are omitted.
An availability guard controls the offered action set. Required verification belongs in deterministic procedure logic and must also be enforced by the business service.
Bind trusted account context rather than allowing model extraction to establish authority. No email-found lookup alone is sufficient authentication.

slides.purpose: Make ordered state transitions concrete.
talk: This is an interactive constructed trace. Advance through owners and watch both ledger entries.
In the favorable path the customer confirms the invoice explanation. Without confirmation or another declared resolution condition, it stays open.
An accepted handoff records ownership and work remaining; it should not be counted as a resolved task.
slides.transition: Now design the non-happy paths.

slides.title: Failure routes are part of the program
slides.body:
Contract failure

Invalid output

Validate the result before branching. Use a defined fallback.

Dependency failure

Timeout

Bound retries and retain every pending obligation.

Authority boundary

Unauthorized write

The service rejects the action under current policy.

Side effect

Repeated write

Use transaction safeguards; record the actual result.
slides.purpose: Connect reliability to failure contracts.
talk: A graph needs meaningful timeout, invalid-output, and handoff routes rather than a default business action.
A resumed workflow can reuse a recorded decision, but this alone does not guarantee exactly-once external side effects.
Transaction-specific safeguards belong in the service performing the write. Recovery must retain the unfinished tasks.
slides.transition: A valid decision can still be semantically wrong.

slides.title: Confidence needs evidence in your domain
slides.body:
A concentrated distribution

Billing

Illustrative output shape.
The highest option can still be wrong.

Validate locally

Compare signals
with adjudicated labels.

Choose gates on development data.
Report error alongside coverage.

Identity, permissions, and policy
remain separate checks.
slides.purpose: Distinguish signal concentration from correctness and permission.
talk: TypeSafe defines Choice and Score confidence from distribution concentration. Noul has no separate confidence field.
The picture is schematic and does not display a returned koa-action distribution. Any provider signal needs a specified meaning and local validation.
A score cannot authorize a business action. Numerical gates are application operating points, not universal constants.
slides.transition: Explore what a stricter gate does to a small labeled sample.

slides.title: A stricter gate moves work somewhere
slides.body:
Twelve labeled examples

✓ correct route · × wrong route
Faded examples go to review.

Synthetic sample / uncalibrated signal
—Coverage
—Auto error
—To review

Inspect the high-scoring mistake.
A stricter gate need not remove it.
slides.purpose: Teach selection, error rate, and coverage without fabricated evidence.
talk: All twelve cases and their scores are constructed teaching data. The signal is uncalibrated and is not a real koa-action field.
Automatic coverage is accepted cases divided by twelve. Automatic error uses only accepted cases; at zero accepted cases it is undefined.
A high-scoring error remains when the threshold rises. Escalations still consume capacity, and errors need not decline monotonically on this sample.
slides.transition: Next account for the work that the routing gate adds and avoids.
slides.status: Synthetic teaching data; drag the threshold

slides.title: Avoided work must exceed added work
slides.body:
Normalized decision-path model
Baseline = G
Candidate = D + O + pG

G = 1.00 generative-stage unit
D = 0.03 decision cost
O = 0.04 orchestration overhead

Baseline
Candidate
73% lower

0.27 normalized units

Break-even: D + O < (1 − p)G
Excludes changed service and human costs.
slides.purpose: Explain conditional economics with transparent algebra.
talk: The numbers are arbitrary normalized units for illustration, not prices, measurements, or a koa-action performance estimate.
The model assumes the same generative-stage cost G whenever invoked. Candidate cost is decision cost plus added orchestration plus p times G.
When p approaches one, the added decision can make the path more expensive. Evaluate whole-case costs separately, including tools, retries, human handling, and unresolved obligations.
slides.transition: Inference latency has an equally important boundary.

slides.title: Fast inference helps the path that uses it
slides.body:
Fast decisionMeasure call latency
Authorized lookupRequired dependency
ExplanationMeasure response latency
Review queue + human handlingCan dominate the time to resolution
Track decision time, response time, and time to completed service separately.
slides.purpose: Separate primitive speed from workflow speed.
talk: Specialized inference can shorten a repeated semantic step. A faster classifier does not by itself establish faster service resolution.
Client-observed call latency includes transport and retries; parallel branches affect critical-path duration differently from serial dependencies.
Measure distribution tails as well as typical latency at the relevant load. Include unfinished cases when reporting resolution, rather than averaging completed cases alone.
slides.transition: Apply the control model to a deliberately incomplete design.

slides.title: Find the missing boundary
slides.body:
Credit requestedStrong model score
Issue creditBusiness transaction

Verify access

Trusted principal and account context.

Check policy

Required procedure before the action.

Enforce in service

Recheck authorization and record outcome.
slides.purpose: Check whether the learner can separate prediction from authority.
talk: Allow a short pause before revealing the repair. The initial diagram is intentionally incomplete.
The strongest answer identifies both authored ordering and independent backend enforcement. Raising the classifier threshold alone does not repair the design.
Also retain pending tasks and specify a bounded fallback. A credit operation has consequences outside the model response.
slides.transition: Training examples must respect the same decision boundaries.

slides.body:

slides.purpose: Prevent future information leaking into model features.
talk: Freeze the source snapshot and reconstruct what the routing node could actually access at the timestamp.
Use independently adjudicated route labels, including mixed and unclear cases. Reviewers labeling the next step see the decision-time evidence.
Record redaction, filtering, and derived examples. Preserving the source does not mean transformations leave the model-visible distribution unchanged.
slides.transition: Separate fitting and selection from final evaluation.

slides.title: Build a pipeline that protects the test
slides.body:
Group before augmentation.

Test a frozen candidate.

Pilot before wider rollout.
slides.purpose: Explain the complete leakage-resistant task-development pipeline.
talk: This is a proposed development pipeline, not koa-action pretraining. Direct adaptation is optional and conditional on supported access.
Train data fits permitted components. Development data uses separate calibration and gate-selection subsets. Locked test data evaluates the frozen model and policy.
Offline gates qualify the candidate for a randomized service pilot. Broader rollout needs pilot quality and economic evidence; reviewed feedback enters only a future dataset.
slides.transition: The split itself must match the deployment claim.
slides.status: Proposed task development; adaptation only where supported

slides.purpose: Distinguish independent cases from repeated observations.
talk: Unseen-account performance and future-traffic performance are different claims and may need separate tests.
Assign related cases and near duplicates together, and generate training augmentations only after partitioning.
One conversation evaluated many times still represents one customer situation. Repeated judgments estimate repeatability, not generalization over new cases.
slides.transition: Define what evidence would earn a rollout.

slides.title: Predeclare what would earn a rollout
slides.body:
Must pass

Quality

Upper uncertainty bound on failure-rate increase

< allowed margin

Must pass

Cost

Lower uncertainty bound on saving per incoming case

> required gain

Must pass

Consequences

Separate limits for harmful actions, assessed on fixed cohorts.

Must pass

Latency

Required response and resolution constraints, including unfinished cases.
slides.purpose: Make reliability and cost a joint acceptance question.
talk: The null is unacceptable quality loss OR insufficient saving. A nonsignificant quality difference does not establish acceptable equivalence.
Define a failed case as an incorrect outcome or any requested task unresolved by the fixed deadline. Count every incoming case once.
Choose sample size and uncertainty methods before testing. Define consequential-error cohorts from independent evidence, not each model’s selected action branch.
slides.transition: Use offline and service experiments for different questions.
slides.status: Proposed acceptance criteria; no measured intervals

slides.title: Evaluate the decision, then the service
slides.body:
Paired offline comparison

Evaluate the decision.

Same held-out snapshots.
Same route question.
Fixed permissions and tools.

Each model’s gate is selected
on development data.

Controlled service pilot

Evaluate the complete case.

Randomized case/account assignment.
Consistent treatment and horizon.
Costs, queues, and unresolved work.

Pilot evidence must precede
wider rollout.
slides.purpose: Prevent offline results being overextended to service economics.
talk: Offline replay isolates the bounded decision. It cannot estimate how changed dialogue affects customers or how escalations affect queue capacity.
In the pilot, keep assignment stable and account for related cases and interference through shared queues. Use the same observation horizon in both arms.
Report observed operating cost per incoming case with resolution and coverage. Disclose setup and maintenance costs separately; total ownership estimates need an explicit volume and horizon.
slides.transition: When an outcome fails, diagnose the responsible boundary.

slides.title: Diagnose the boundary that failed
slides.body:
Invoice explained; outage lostInspect the recorded route and state changes
Route = billingDecision boundaryInspect input evidence,
labels, and category definition.
Route = mixedWorkflow boundaryInspect the transition that
dropped the pending task.
Trace looks correctOutcome boundaryInspect services and the
resolution condition.
slides.purpose: Connect disaggregation to targeted learning from failure.
talk: A wrong route can motivate better decision data. A correct mixed route followed by dropped state calls for a workflow repair.
Offline semantic judges can prioritize traces, but require validation against independent references. Repeatability is a separate property from correctness.
Sample apparent successes as well as escalations. A post-run evaluation score cannot prevent an action that has already happened.

slides.purpose: Give the audience a bounded practical next step.
talk: The tutorial’s central claim is an allocation principle: specialize judgment where it earns its place, retain general reasoning where needed, and make control explicit.
Predictable contracts and runtime paths create an inspectable system; correctness and economics still require evidence from complete cases.
The next engineering artifact is a decision contract and a small graph, followed by held-out evaluation and a controlled pilot.
